beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three friends share half a pound of chocolate. How much does each friend get?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A cook has two cups of raisins. Each serving is one third of a cup. How many servings?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Both answers should be small, because we're dividing.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Let's see. One answer measures a share. The other counts servings.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: This outline is a whole one-pound chocolate bar. We have just half of it.

do.text: Half a pound shared by 3 friends.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cut our half into three equal pieces.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Is each piece one third of a pound?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One third of our half. To name it in pounds, compare it with the whole bar.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Imagine the same cuts in the missing half. Three here, three there. Six equal pieces would fill one pound.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So each friend gets one sixth of a pound.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three small shares put together give back our half pound.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: For the raisins, each strip represents one cup. There are two cups altogether.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One serving is a third of a cup. Three equal servings fit in one cup.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: And three fit in the other cup.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Count the servings. Three. Six.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Six servings! The number is bigger than two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes. We still have two cups of raisins. Six counts the smaller servings.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Check: six servings of one third cup make two cups.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Same division sign, two questions. How big is each share? How many servings fit?

do.text: Size of a share, or number of shares?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: A sixth of a pound is a size. Six servings is a count.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Halves and thirds are unit fractions: one of the equal parts that make a whole.

do.meaning: One equal part of a whole; 1 on top.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Share one third of a liter equally among four people. What goes in each equation box?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One third is the amount. Four is the number of people.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cut the third into four equal shares. Imagine doing that to all three thirds.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three rows of four: twelve equal pieces in a liter. Each person gets one twelfth.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Twelve names how many pieces fill the whole liter. Our answer is the size of just one.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The answer to division is called the quotient. Check it by multiplying by the number we divided by.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four twelfths join back into one third. The check product is our starting amount.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four liters fill containers that each hold one fifth of a liter. How many containers?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Each liter fills five containers.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Five. Ten. Fifteen. Twenty.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four groups of five. Twenty containers.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: To check, multiply twenty by the size of each container. What amount should we get back?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four liters.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Try half a liter shared equally among four people. Picture each half cut into four.

do.text: Half a liter shared by 4 people.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Eight equal pieces in one liter. One eighth of a liter each.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three liters, poured into quarter-liter cups. How many cups?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four cups per liter. Three times four is twelve cups.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A trail is four miles long. One track lap is half a mile. How many laps cover the same distance?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Start with four miles. Divide by half a mile per lap.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Two laps per mile. Four miles take eight laps.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Which question is this? A quarter yard of ribbon is cut into two equal lengths for bows.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Sharing. We know there are two bows. We need the length for each.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Split the quarter in two. Eight equal lengths would make a yard.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One eighth yard per bow.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: And this? Two yards of ribbon. Each bow needs a quarter yard.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Counting. We know the length for each bow. How many fit?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four in each yard. Eight bows.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One eighth yard, or eight bows. The story tells me what the answer means.

do.text: Name the unit of your answer.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Division asks how big each share is, or how many shares fit.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Multiply the answer by what you divided by. You should recover the starting amount.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Share a piece among several people, and the pieces get smaller. Count pieces smaller than one whole, and the number gets bigger. Multiply to check.
